passage:
Wednesday night. Eshaan missed the third deadline this month. The old me would have sent a sharp email. Instead I asked Eshaan to walk with me after lunch and said, "You've always been careful. I've noticed the last three slipped, and I'm wondering what's getting in the way."

Eshaan went quiet, then said things at home have been heavy and the mornings are chaos. I didn't pry. I asked what would help, and Eshaan asked to shift the start time by an hour. We agreed on smaller milestones with a Friday check-in, and I said clearly that the report still has to be in by the twentieth.

Kindness and accountability had to sit together. I'm a bit proud, and a bit tired.

Chinmay

qa.q: What did Eshaan ask to change?
qa.a: Eshaan asked to shift the start time by an hour.

qa.q: What does Chinmay suspect is behind Eshaan's missed deadlines, and why ask instead of scold?
qa.a: Chinmay suspects something in Eshaan's life is getting in the way, so asks rather than assuming carelessness; afterwards Chinmay feels a bit proud, and a bit tired, at holding kindness and accountability together.

qa.q: How did Chinmay combine kindness with accountability?
qa.a: Chinmay asked privately, agreed a later start time, set smaller milestones with Friday check-ins and kept the deadline clear.

qa.q: How might Eshaan have felt being asked instead of scolded?
qa.a: Probably relieved and safer to be honest, since Eshaan opened up and asked for what would help.

grounding: A junior keeps missing deadlines and Chinmay senses something is going on, asks privately, adjusts support and keeps expectations clear.

passage:
It was the last week of the quarter, the Pune office was short of three people, and Tenzin had missed his third deadline in a month. Himani had a report due to the regional head on Friday. She was tempted to send Tenzin a sharp email and take the work herself.

Instead she asked him to walk with her to the tea stall downstairs. "You've been great for a year. Something's different lately. What's getting in the way?"

Tenzin stared at his cup. "My father's in the hospital in Siliguri. I'm on the phone with my sister every night. I didn't want to use it as an excuse."

Himani felt her irritation drain away. "I'm sorry. Thank you for telling me."

They agreed: for the next month, he would do only the supplier reports, no client calls, with a check-in every Monday and Thursday. "If a deadline won't work, tell me the day before, not the day after," she said. He nodded, and met every one.

qa.q: Where was Tenzin's father in the hospital?
qa.a: His father was in the hospital in Siliguri.

qa.q: How did Himani feel when Tenzin explained?
qa.a: Himani felt her irritation drain away and felt sympathy for him.

qa.q: How did Himani combine kindness with clear expectations?
qa.a: She asked privately what was wrong, reduced his workload for a month, and set clear check-ins and a rule to flag problems a day early.

qa.q: How might Tenzin have felt carrying his father's illness silently at work?
qa.a: Tenzin likely felt stretched thin and anxious, not wanting to seem to make excuses.

grounding: The story shows a manager whose junior keeps missing deadlines, who asks privately what is getting in the way, adjusts support and sets clear expectations.

passage:
At the architecture firm in Baner, Lakshmi had missed two drawings in two weeks. She had been one of the sharpest juniors when she joined. Now she came in late, left early, and answered emails at midnight.

Sunaina, her manager, could feel the partners watching. She was frustrated, and a little worried.

On Wednesday she booked the small meeting room. "Lakshmi, your work used to be spot on. What's getting in the way?"

Lakshmi's eyes filled. "My son's crèche closed. My mother-in-law helps, but only till four. I've been working after he sleeps."

Sunaina nodded slowly. "Okay. Thank you for telling me. Let's fix the schedule, not you."

They agreed Lakshmi would work eight to four, and take the site visits only on Saturdays when her husband was home. Sunaina was clear too: "The Tuesday drawings still need to be on time. If something slips, tell me early." Lakshmi nodded. The next Tuesday, the drawing was in by noon.

qa.q: How many drawings had Lakshmi missed in two weeks?
What was Sunaina feeling before the Wednesday talk?
qa.a: Sunaina felt frustrated and a little worried, aware the partners were watching.

qa.q: Which of Sunaina's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking privately and warmly revealed the real problem, and changing the schedule while keeping clear deadlines let kindness and accountability work together.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel when Sunaina asked what was wrong?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt overwhelmed and relieved to be asked, her eyes filling with tears.

grounding: The passage shows a manager whose junior keeps missing deadlines, who asks privately what is wrong, adjusts support and keeps clear expectations.
